os_classification.instructions: Put the software component in `component` (described in `description`) into the group whose definition it matches. A component that matches an OS definition is OS even if it looks like an application, library or driver. A role rather than a product (any application or library that does something) is classified as the kind of software it refers to.

criteria.OS: Part of an operating system: (1) the operating system, its kernel and every kernel module, subsystem, file system and driver that ships with the kernel or the operating system, including bundled drivers for third-party hardware; (2) components built into the operating system and not released separately: built-in apps, accessories, frameworks, shell, services, server roles and optional features, legacy built-in browser and scripting engines, built-in data-access and XML components, built-in antimalware protection, and anything named or described as a library, handler, service or component of the operating system; (3) a distribution's base system: C library, shells, privilege and authentication tools, init, device and system daemons, time synchronization, printing system and filters, display server and graphics stack, SSH server and agent, core command-line, file, disk and storage utilities, and package-management and distribution tools; (4) the firmware or system image of a network, security, traffic-handling, storage, embedded or operational-technology device (firewall, VPN gateway, load balancer, application delivery controller, router, switch, phone, NAS, controller) or of a bare-metal hypervisor, under any product name, including every service, protocol and interface inside it; (5) hardware, processor and architecture conditions (CPU, GPU, TPM, microcode).
criteria.Non-OS: Not part of an operating system: (1) standalone applications, servers and services, including separately released products of the operating system vendor and apps updated through an app store, including the app store itself and system components updated through it, even when preinstalled; (2) general-purpose libraries, packages, plugins, extensions and frameworks (cryptography, compression, parsing, image, media, networking and others), even when a distribution also ships them; (3) network servers for web, mail, DNS, database, messaging and file sharing, other than the operating system's own server roles; (4) language runtimes, interpreters, virtual machines, browsers and browser engines; (5) drivers and agents installed from a hardware or software vendor; (6) management, business and security applications that run on a server, a virtual machine or a virtual appliance.
